rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Drift velocity is very slow ($10^{-4}$ m/s) but the signal (electric field) travels at nearly the speed of light. These are two entirely different things — electrons don't race from switch to bulb; the field establishes itself instantly.  ·  The magnitude of current $I$ is the same everywhere in a series circuit. Current is not consumed — electrons drift at the same average speed everywhere, just as water flows at the same rate through a pipe of uniform cross-section.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: A larger cross-sectional area means more charge carriers can flow simultaneously, so for the same current, the drift velocity decreases: $v_d = I/(nAe)$. A thick wire carries current with slower drift velocity than a thin wire of the same material.  ·  The thermal speed of electrons ($\sim 10^5$ m/s) is about $10^9$ times the drift velocity ($\sim 10^{-4}$ m/s). The thermal motion is random and contributes no net current; only the drift component does.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Drift velocity in a typical copper wire is only about $0.1$ mm/s — a snail is millions of times faster than the electrons carrying current.  ·  Despite the slow drift of electrons, the electric field propagates at a significant fraction of the speed of light ($\sim 2 \times 10^8$ m/s in typical wires), which is why lights turn on instantly.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Current $I$:** rate of flow of charge. $I = Q/t$. Units: ampere (A).  ·  **Conventional current:** flows from positive to negative. Electron flow is opposite, from negative to positive.  ·  **Drift velocity $v_d$:** the average velocity of free electrons in a conductor under an electric field. It is very slow, about $10^{-4}\,\text{m/s}$.
